extraction_notes.note: The source has many unfinished or run-on sentences ("$i<n$ and" then a new paragraph; "Such an $\bold M$ exists It is"; "consists of those diagrams," then "and finally"), so these prose nodes absorb the next fragment or end without a period.

The argument in Section 3.2 that starts "Assume for contradiction" is incomplete (the needed condition on $k$ is posed as an open question in the middle). I took it as a proof of ClP10, stated right after it, with OpenP2 nested inside.
Theorem 4.1 is a simplified version of Andreka-Nemeti's construction, and Corollary 4.3(1) is Monk's classical result. Both are marked external, with the paper's proofs as paper.

The neat embedding theorem ($\sf RRA=\bigcap_k S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}$) is stated in full only inside the sentence that applies it. Under the whole-sentence rule it stays part of ClP9 and gets no node of its own.
The proof of Corollary 4.3 has paragraphs for 'the second' item and for 'the cylindric case', but none for item (1).

nodes.name: Atom structure (convention)
nodes.statement: In what follows, by an atom structure, we mean an atom structure of any class of completely additive Boolean algebras.
nodes.genus: atom structure of any class of completely additive Boolean algebras

nodes.name: Splitting, blur, blown up and blurred atom structure; weak and strong atom structures
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item A splitting of $N$ is a disjoint union $N\times I$, where $I$ is an infinite set. \item A blur for $N$ is any set $J$. \item An atom structure $\alpha$ is blown up and blurred if, there exists a subset $J'$ of a set $J$ of blurs, possibly empty, such that $\alpha$ has underlying set $X=N\times I \times J'$; the latter atom structure is called a blur of $N$ via $J$, and is denoted by $\alpha(N,J).$ Furthermore, every $j\in J$, induces a non-principal ultrafilter in $\wp(X)$. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N, J)$ reflects $N$, if $N$ is faithfully represented in ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\alpha(N,J)$ \item An atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$ is weak if ${\mathfrak{Tm}}\alpha(N,J)$ is representable. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N, J)$ is very weak ${\mathfrak{Tm}}\alpha(N,J)$ is not representable. \item An atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$ is strong if ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\alpha(N,J)$ is representable. \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: Splitting $N\times I$ of a graph $N$, blurs $J$, the blown-up-and-blurred atom structure $\alpha(N,J)$ on $N\times I\times J'$, and when it is weak (term algebra representable) or strong (complex algebra representable).

nodes.name: Graph G
nodes.statement: Let ${\bf G}$ be a graph.

nodes.name: Labelled graphs F (labels)
nodes.statement: One can define a family of labelled graphs $\cal F$ such that every edge of each graph $\Gamma\in {\cal F}$, is labelled by a unique label from ${\bf G}\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, $\rho\notin {\bf G}$, in a carefully chosen way.
differentia: every edge of each graph $\Gamma\in {\cal F}$, is labelled by a unique label from ${\bf G}\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, $\rho\notin {\bf G}$

nodes.name: Colour of (rho, i)
nodes.statement: The colour of $(\rho, i)$ is defined to be $i$.

nodes.name: Colour of (a, i)
nodes.statement: The \textit{colour} of $(a, i)$ for $a \in {\bf G}$ is $i$.

nodes.name: The class F of labelled graphs
nodes.statement: $\cal F$ consists of all complete labelled graphs $\Gamma$ (possibly the empty graph) such that for all distinct $ x, y, z \in \Gamma$, writing $ (a, i) = \Gamma (y, x)$, $ (b, j) = \Gamma (y, z)$, $ (c,l) = \Gamma (x, z)$, we have:\\ \begin{enumarab} \item $| \{ i, j, l \} > 1 $, or \item $ a, b, c \in {\bf G}$ and $ \{ a, b, c \} $ has at least one edge of ${\bf G}$, or \item exactly one of $a, b, c$ -- say, $a$ -- is $\rho$, and $bc$ is an edge of ${\bf G}$, or \item two or more of $a, b, c$ are $\rho$. \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: $\cal F$: complete labelled graphs in which every triangle either has at least two colours, or contains a $\bf G$-edge, or has the prescribed $\rho$ pattern.

nodes.name: Labelled graph M
nodes.statement: One forms a labelled graph $M$ which can be viewed as model of a natural signature, namely, the one with relation symbols $R_{(a, i)}$, for each $a \in {\bf G} \cup \{\rho\}$, $i<n$ and Then one takes a subset $W\subseteq {}^nM$, by roughly dropping assignments that do not satify $(\rho, l)$ for every $l<n$.
nodes.statement_short: $M$: a labelled graph (Fraisse limit of $\cal F$) viewed as a model with relation symbols $R_{(a,i)}$; one then restricts assignments.

nodes.name: Set of permitted assignments W
nodes.statement: Formally, $W = \{ \bar{a} \in {}^n M : M \models ( \bigwedge_{i < j < n, l < n} \neg (\rho, l)(x_i, x_j))(\bar{a}) \}.$
nodes.statement_short: $W$: the $n$-tuples of $M$ no two of whose elements are joined by a $\rho$-labelled edge.

nodes.name: The relativized set algebra on W is atomic and representable
nodes.statement: Now for particular choices of ${\bf G}$; for example if ${\bf G}$ is a certain rainbow graph, or more simply a countable infinite collection of pairwise union of disjoint $N$ cliques with $N\geq n(n-1)/2$, or is the graph whose nodes are the natural numbers, and the edge relation is defined by $iEj$ iff $0<|i-j|<N$, for same $N.$ Here, the choice of $N$ is not haphazard, but it a bound of edges of complete graphs having $n$ nodes. The relativized set algebras based on $M$, but permitting as assignments satisfying formulas only $n$ sequences in $W$ will be an atomic representable algebra.
assumptions: ${\bf G}$ is a certain rainbow graph, or more simply a countable infinite collection of pairwise union of disjoint $N$ cliques with $N\geq n(n-1)/2$
conclusions: The relativized set algebras based on $M$, but permitting as assignments satisfying formulas only $n$ sequences in $W$ will be an atomic representable algebra.
nodes.statement_short: For suitable $\bf G$ (disjoint $N$-cliques, $N\geq n(n-1)/2$), the set algebra on $M$ relativized to $W$ is atomic and representable.

nodes.name: The set algebra A and phi^M
nodes.statement: This algebr, call it ${\mathfrak{A}}$, has universe $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n\}$ where $\phi^M=\{s\in W: M\models \phi[s]\}.$ (This is not representable by its definition because its unit is not a square.) Here $\phi^M$ denotes the permitted asignments satisfyng $\phi$ in $M$.

nodes.name: The completion C is not representable
nodes.statement: Its completion is the relativized set algebra ${\mathfrak{C}}$ with universe the larger $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n_{\infty,\omega}\}$, which turns out not representable.
assumptions: Its completion is the relativized set algebra ${\mathfrak{C}}$ with universe the larger $\{\phi^M: \phi\in L^n_{\infty,\omega}\}$
conclusions: which turns out not representable

nodes.name: Cm At A is isomorphic to C
nodes.statement: The isomorphism from ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\sf At}{\mathfrak{A}}$ to ${\mathfrak{C}}$ is given by $X\mapsto \bigcup X$.
conclusions: The isomorphism from ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\sf At}{\mathfrak{A}}$ to ${\mathfrak{C}}$ is given by $X\mapsto \bigcup X$.

nodes.name: First construction as split and blur
nodes.statement: Take the $n$ disjoint copies of $N\times \omega={\bf G}$. Let $a\in {\bf G}\times n$. Then $a\in N\times \omega\times n$. Then for every $(a,i)$ where $a\in N\times \omega$, and $i<n$, we have an atom $R_{a,i}^{{\mathfrak{M}}}\in {\mathfrak{A}}$. The term algebra of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ is generated by those. Hence ${\mathfrak{N}}\times \omega\times n$ is the atom structure of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ which can be weakly represented using the $n$ blurs, namely the set $\{\rho, i): i<n\}$. The clique $N$ appeas on the complex algebra level, forcing a finite $N$ colouring, so that the complex algebra cannot be representable.
nodes.statement_short: Hodkinson's construction recast: atoms $N\times\omega\times n$, $n$ blurs $(\rho,i)$ represent the term algebra, while the clique $N$ reappears in the complex algebra and blocks representability.

nodes.name: Infinite N gives complete representability
nodes.statement: We note that if $N$ is infinite, then the complex algebra (which is the completion of the algebra constructed as above ) will be representable and so ${\mathfrak{A}}$, together the term algebra will be completely representable.
conclusions: the complex algebra (which is the completion of the algebra constructed as above ) will be representable and so ${\mathfrak{A}}$, together the term algebra will be completely representable

nodes.name: Relation algebra atom structure alpha(G)
nodes.statement: We define a relation algebra atom structure $\alpha({\bf G})$ of the form $(\{1'\}\cup ({\bf G}\times n), R_{1'}, \breve{R}, R_;)$. The only identity atom is $1'$. All atoms are self converse, so $\breve{R}=\{(a, a): a \text { an atom }\}.$

nodes.name: Colour of an atom of alpha(G)
nodes.statement: The colour of an atom $(a,i)\in {\bf G}\times n$ is $i$. The identity $1'$ has no colour.

nodes.name: Consistent triple of atoms
nodes.statement: A triple $(a,b,c)$ of atoms in $\alpha({\bf G})$ is consistent if $R;(a,b,c)$ holds.

nodes.name: Consistent triples of alpha(G)
nodes.statement: Then the consistent triples are $(a,b,c)$ where \begin{itemize} \item one of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and the other two are equal, or \item none of $a,b,c$ is $1'$ and they do not all have the same colour, or \item $a=(a', i), b=(b', i)$ and $c=(c', i)$ for some $i<n$ and $a',b',c'\in {\bf G}$, and there exists at least one graph edge of $G$ in $\{a', b', c'\}$. \end{itemize}
conclusions: the consistent triples are $(a,b,c)$ where
nodes.statement_short: The consistent triples: identity with two equal atoms, non-monochromatic triples, or monochromatic triples containing a $\bf G$-edge.

nodes.name: alpha(G) is a relation atom structure
nodes.statement: $\alpha({\bf G})$ can be checked to be a relation atom structure.
conclusions: $\alpha({\bf G})$ can be checked to be a relation atom structure.

nodes.name: At A is isomorphic to the basic matrices M_n over alpha(G)
nodes.statement: This allows the relation algebra to have an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis and, in fact, the atom structure of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ is isomorphic (as a cylindric algebra atom structure) to the atom structure ${\cal M}_n$ of all $n$-dimensional basic matrices over the relation algebra atom structure $\alpha({\bf G})$.
conclusions: the relation algebra to have an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis

the atom structure of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ is isomorphic (as a cylindric algebra atom structure) to the atom structure ${\cal M}_n$ of all $n$-dimensional basic matrices over the relation algebra atom structure $\alpha({\bf G})$
nodes.statement_short: Using $n$ colours gives $\alpha({\bf G})$ an $n$-dimensional cylindric basis, and At$\mathfrak A$ is isomorphic to the basic-matrix atom structure ${\cal M}_n$.

nodes.name: Proof that At A is isomorphic to M_n
nodes.statement: Indeed, for each $m \in {\cal M}_n, \,\ \textrm{let} \,\ \alpha_m = \bigwedge_{i,j<n} \alpha_{ij}. $ Here $ \alpha_{ij}$ is $x_i = x_j$ if $ m_{ij} = 1$' and $R(x_i, x_j)$ otherwise, where $R = m_{ij} \in L$. Then the map $(m \mapsto \alpha^W_m)_{m \in {\cal M}_n}$ is a well - defined isomorphism of $n$-dimensional cylindric algebra atom structures.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the explicit map $m\mapsto\alpha_m^W$ from basic matrices to conjunctions of atomic formulas and assert it is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Complex algebra of alpha(G) is not representable (chromatic number N)
nodes.statement: It can be shown that the complex algebras of this atom structure is not representable, because its chromatic number is finite; indeed it is exactly $N$. (This will be demonstrated below.)
conclusions: the complex algebras of this atom structure is not representable

nodes.name: Is the constructed relation algebra outside SRaCA_{n+2}?
nodes.statement: Is it possible, thatthe constructed relation algebrais {\it not} in $S{\sf Ra} {\sf CA}_{n+2}$ which is strictly smaller that ${\sf RRA}$.

nodes.name: Finite-infinite discrepancy for any representation
nodes.statement: In any event, there is a finite-infinite discrepancy here, as well, no matter what kind of representation we consider, the base has to be infinite. A representation maps the complex algebra into the powerset of a set of ordered pairs, with base $X$, thae latter has to be infinite. At the same time the graph has an $N$ coloring, and this can be used to partition the complex algebra into $(N\times n)+1$ blocks.
nodes.statement_short: Any representation has infinite base, while the $N$-colouring partitions the complex algebra into $N\times n+1$ blocks.

nodes.name: Why the classical argument fails for relativized representations
nodes.statement: But this is not enough; the idea in the classical case, works because one member of the partition induced by the finite colouring will be monochromatic, and will satisfy $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$, which is a contradiction. The last condition is not guaranteed when we have only relativized representations, because if $h$ is such a representation, it is not really a faithful one, in the sense that it can happen that there are $x_0, x_1,x_2\in X$, and $(x_0,x_1)\in h(a)$, $(x_1, x_2)\in h(b)$, $(x_0, x_2)\in h(c)$, and $a, b, c\in {\mathfrak{Cm}}{\bf G}$, but $h((a;b).c)=0$ if the node $x_1$ witnessing composition, lies outside the $n$ clique determined by $x_0, x_2$, This cannot happen in case of classical representation.
nodes.statement_short: Classically a monochromatic block $P$ satisfies $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$, a contradiction; relativized representations need not witness composition, so this fails.

nodes.name: Complex algebra not in SRaCA_{n+k} for some k
nodes.statement: But we are also {\it certain } that the complex algebra is not in $S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}$ for some $k\in \omega$, by the neat embedding theorem for relation algebras, namey, ${\sf RRA}=\bigcap_{k\in \omega}S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}.$
conclusions: the complex algebra is not in $S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}$ for some $k\in \omega$
nodes.statement_short: Since $\sf RRA=\bigcap_k S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}$ (neat embedding theorem) and the complex algebra is non-representable, it lies outside some $S{\sf Ra}{\sf CA}_{n+k}$.

nodes.name: Clique of a relativized representation
nodes.statement: A clique $C$ of $X$ is a subset of the domain $X$, that can indeed be viewed as a complete graph, in the sense that any two points in it we have $X\models 1(x,y)$, equivalently $(x,y)\in V$, where $V$ is the unit of the relativization.

nodes.name: n+k squareness
nodes.statement: The property of $n+k$ squareness means, then for all cliques $C$ of $X$ with $|C|<n+k$, can always be extended to another clique having at most one more element witnessing composition, so that composition can be preserved in the representation, but only locally.
nodes.statement_short: $n+k$-square: every clique of size $<n+k$ can be extended by one node witnessing any composition.

nodes.name: Hodkinson's theorem on non-representable completions
nodes.statement: Let ${\bf G}$ be a graph that is a disjoint union of cliques having size $n$. Then there is a strongly $n$ homogenious labelled graph $M$, every edge is labelled by an element from ${\bf G}\cup \{\rho\}\times n$, $W\subseteq {}^nM$, such that the set algebra based on $W$ is an atomic ${\mathfrak{A}}\in {\sf RCA}_n$, and there is an atomic ${\sf R}\in {\sf RRA}$ the latter with an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis, such that ${\mathfrak{A}}\cong {\sf Mat}_n{\sf R}$, and the completions of ${\mathfrak{A}}$ and ${\sf R}$ are not representable, hence they are not completely representable.

there is an atomic ${\sf R}\in {\sf RRA}$ the latter with an $n$ dimensional cylindric basis, such that ${\mathfrak{A}}\cong {\sf Mat}_n{\sf R}$

nodes.name: Consistent triples of the blow up and blur atom structure
nodes.statement: Let $i,j,k\in \omega$, $P,Q,R\in I$ and $S,Z,W\in J$ such that $P\in S$, $Q\in Z$ and $R\in W$. Then the triple $(a_i^{P,S},a_j^{Q,Z}, a_k^{R,W})$ is consistent iff either \begin{enumroman} \item $S\cap Z\cap W=\emptyset,$ or \item $e(i,j,k)\&P\leq Q;R.$ \end{enumroman}
nodes.statement_short: A triple of atoms is consistent iff their blurs have empty common intersection, or the rows are evenly distributed and $P\leq Q;R$ in $\bold M$.

${\cal R}$ the term algebra over $\cal F$ is representable.
nodes.statement_short: The complex algebra over $\cal F$ is a non-representable relation algebra, while its term algebra is representable.

nodes.name: Proof of the blow up and blur theorem
nodes.statement: \begin{enumarab} \item Non representabiliy uses the first partition of $H$. Note that $;$ is defined on ${\mathfrak{Cm}}({\cal F})$ so that $$H^P; H^Q=\bigcup \{H^Z: Z\leq P; Q\in {\bold M}\}.$$ So $\bold M$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of ${\mathfrak{Cm}} F$. But ${\mathfrak{Cm}} F$ can only be represented on infinite sets, while ${\mathfrak{M}}$ only on finite ones, hence we are done. \item The representability of the term algebra uses the second partition. The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$. For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $${\sf Uf}=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ ${\sf Uf}$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$. Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$ So to represent $\cal R$ using $Uf$ as colours, we want to achieve (i) -(iii) below: \begin{enumroman} \item $(U^a,U^b,U^W)$ is consistent whenever $a,b\in H$ and $a;b\in U^W.$ \item $(F,G,K)$ is consistent whenever at least two of $F,G,K$ are non-principal and $F,G,K\in Uf-\{U^{Id}\}.$ \item For any $a,b,c,d\in H$, there is $W\in J'$ such that $a;b\cap c;d\in U^W$. \end{enumroman} Let us see how to represent this algebra. We call $(G,l)$ a {\it consistent coloured graph} if $G$ is a set, $l:G\times G\to Uf$ such that for all $x,y,z\in G$, the following hold: \begin{enumroman} \item $l(x,y)=U^{Id}$ iff $x=y,$ \item $l(x,y)=l(y,x)$ \item The triple $(l(x,y),l(x,z),l(y,z))$ is consistent. \end{enumroman} We say that a consistent coloured graph $(G,l)$ is complete if for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$. We will build a complete consistent graph step-by-step. So assume (inductively) that$(G,l)$ is a consistent coloured graph and $(l(x,y), F, K)$ is a consistent triple. We shall extend $(G,l)$ with a new point $z$ such that $(l(x,y), l(z,x), l(z,y)) =(l(x,y),G,K).$ Let $z\notin G.$ We define $l(z,p)$ for $p\in G$ as follows: $$l(z,x)=F$$ $$l(z,y)=K, \text { and if } p\in G\smallsetminus \{x,y\}, \text { then }$$ $$l(z,p)=U^W\text { for some }W\in J' \text { such that both }$$ $$(U^W, F, l(x,p))\text { and } (U^W, K, l(y,p))\text { are consistent }.$$ Such a $W$ exists by our assumptions (i)-(iii). Conditions (i)-(ii) guarantee that this extension is again a consistent coloured graph. We now show that any non-empty complete coloured graph $(G,l)$ gives a representation for $\cal R.$ For any $X\in R$ define $$rep(X)=\{(u,v)\in G\times G: X\in l(u,v)\}$$ We show that $$rep:{\cal R}\to R(G)$$ is an embedding. $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism because all the labels are ultrafilters. $$rep(Id)=\{(u,u): u\in G\},$$ and for all $X\in R$, $$rep(X)^{-1}=rep(X).$$ The latter follows from the first condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph. From the second condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph, we have: $$rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y).$$ Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X), (v,w)\in rep(Y)$ I.e. $X\in l(u,v), Y\in l(v,w).$ Since $(l(u,v), l(v,w), l(u,w))$ is consistent, then $X;Y\in l(u,w)$, i.e. $(u,w)\in rep(X;Y).$ On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in {\sf Uf}$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$ Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$ \end{enumarab}
nodes.statement_short: (1) $\bold M$ embeds in ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\cal F$ via $P\mapsto H^P$, clashing finite vs infinite bases. (2) Build a complete consistent coloured graph step by step with ultrafilter labels; it yields a representation $rep$ of $\cal R$.

nodes.name: Analogy between the two constructions
nodes.statement: Replace the clique $N$ in Hodkinson's construction by $\bold M$, in this case the term algebra, $\cal R$ is also obtained by replacing every atom by infinitely many ones, and $\bold M$ appears on the global level as a subalgebra of the complex algebra. To this consruction we can also associate a finite graph with finite chromatic number, namely the complete graph on $\bold M$. The blurs are the colours, that correspond to the colours $(\rho, i)$ in Sayed Ahmed 's construction.

nodes.name: Formal map between the two constructions
nodes.statement: More formally, we define a function that maps the ingredients of the first construction to that of the second: $$N\mapsto \bold M$$ $$N\times \omega\times n\mapsto \omega\times P\times J$$ In the former case $J'=\emptyset$, the blurs do not appear on this level, in the second spliting all blurs are used. $$\{(\rho , i): i<n \}\mapsto \{ W: W\in J\}.$$ Here in the first case $n$ blurs are needed to represent the new term algebra. In the later it is the number of two elements subsets of $J$. For $\phi\in L^+$, let $\phi^M=\{s\in {}^nM: M\models \phi[s]\}.$ Here we are {\it not} relativizing semantics. $$\{{\phi}^M: \phi \in L\}\mapsto {\sf Cof}(E^W)$$ $${\mathfrak{A}}\mapsto {\cal R}$$ $${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\sf At}{\mathfrak{A}}\to {\mathfrak{Cm}}{\sf At}{\cal R}$$

nodes.name: Atom structures F(l, mu)
nodes.statement: Let $l\in \omega$, $l\geq 2$, and let $\mu$ be a non-zero cardinal. Let $I$ be a finite set, $|I|\geq 3l.$ Let $$J=\{(X,n): X\subseteq I, |X|=l,n<\mu\}.$$ Let $H$ be as before, i.e. $$H=\{a_i^{P,W}: i\in \omega, P\in I, W\in J\}.$$ Define $(a_i^{P,S,p}, a_j^{Q,Z,q}, a_k^{R,W,r})$ is consistent ff $S\cap Z\cap W=\emptyset$ or $ e(i,j,k) \text { and } |\{P,Q,R\}|\neq 1.$ Pending on $l$ and $\mu$, let us call these atom structures ${\cal F}(l,\mu).$ Then our first example in is just ${\cal F}(2,1).$ If $\mu\geq \omega$, then $J$ as defined above would be infinite, and ${\sf Uf}$ will be a proper subset of the ultrafilters. It is not difficult to show that if $l\geq \omega$ (and we relax the condition that $I$ be finite), then ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is completely representable, and if $l<\omega$ then ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal F}(l,\mu)$ is not representable. In the former case we have infnitely many colours, so that the chromatic nmber of the graph is infinite, while in the second case the chromatic number is infinite. Informally, if the blurs get arbitarily large, then in the limit, the resulting algebra will be completely representable, and so its complex algebra will be representable. If we take, a sequence of blurs, each finite, but increasing in size we get a sequence of algebras that are not completely representable, and the sequence of their complex algebras will not be representable. The limit of the former, will be completely representable (with an infinite set of blurs); its completion will be the limit of the second sequence of non representable, will be representable. Either construction can be used to achieve this. This phenomena has many reincarnations in the literature. One is the following: It is is nothing more than Monk's classical non finite axiomatizability result; it gives a sequence of non representable algebras whose ultraproduct is completely representable.

nodes.name: Proof of non-finite axiomatizability
nodes.statement: {Proof} For the second we use the second construction. Let ${\cal D}$ be a non- trivial ultraproduct of the atom structures ${\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$. Then ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal D}$ is completely representable. Thus ${\mathfrak{Tm}}{\cal F}(i,1)$ are ${\sf RRA}$'s without a complete representation while their ultraproduct has a complete representation. Also ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$ are non representable with a completely representable ultraproduct. This yields the desired result. We prove the cylindric case. Take ${\bf G}_i$ to be the disjoint union of cliques of size $n(n-1)/2+i$. Let $\alpha_i$ be the corresponding atom astructure of ${\mathfrak{A}}_i$, as constructed above. Then ${\mathfrak{Cm}} {\mathfrak{A}}_i$ is not representable, but $\prod_{i\in \omega}{\mathfrak{Cm}}{\mathfrak{A}}_i={\mathfrak{Cm}}(\prod_{i\in \omega}{\mathfrak{A}}_i)$. Then the latter is based on the disjoint union of the cliques which is arbitrarily large, hence is representable.

nodes.name: Finite partition J
nodes.statement: The nodes of $N\times \omega$ can be partitioned into sets $\{C_j: j<n\}$ such that there are no edges within $C_j$. Let $J=\{1', (C_j,k): j<N, k<n\}$ Then clearly, $\sum J=1$ in ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\alpha({\bf G})$, so that $J$ is partition of ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\alpha({\bf G})$ into $N\times n+1$ blocks.
nodes.statement_short: Partition $\mathfrak{Cm}\alpha(\bf G)$ into $N\times n+1$ blocks $J$.

nodes.name: Apply Ramsey's theorem
nodes.statement: As $J$ is finite, we have for any $x,y\in X$ there is a $P\in J$ with $(x,y)\in h(P)$. Since ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\alpha({\bf G})$ is infinite then $X$ is infinite. Ramsys's theorem aplies in this context, to allow us to infer, that there are distinct $x_i\in X$ $(i<\omega)$, $J\subseteq \omega\times \omega$ infinite and $P\in J$ such that $(x_i, x_j)\in h(P)$ for $(i, j)\in J$, $i\neq j$. Then $P\neq 1'$.
nodes.statement_short: Infinite base plus Ramsey's theorem give an infinite clique monochromatic in some block $P\neq1'$.

nodes.name: Condition needed on k
nodes.statement: The condition we need on $k$, is that if $(x_0, x_1)\in h(a)$, $(x_1, x_2)\in h(b)$ and $(x_0, x_2)\in h(c),$ then $a;b.c\neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: State the condition on $k$ that is needed.

nodes.name: Open question on k
nodes.statement: So this prompts: {\it Find a combinatorial relation between $n,k, N$ with $N\geq n(n-1)/2$ that forces $(P;P)\cdot P\neq 0$. What is the least such $k$? This is formulated for any $P$, but maybe the condition would also force Ramseys theorem to give the right block.}
nodes.statement_short: Pose the problem of finding the combinatorial condition.

nodes.name: Monochromatic P gives (P;P).P = 0
nodes.statement: A non -zero element $a$ of ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\alpha({\bf G})$ is monochromatic, if $a\leq 1'$, or $a\leq (\Gamma,s)$ for some $s<n$. Now $P$ is monochromatic, and the $C_j$ s are independent, it follows also from the definition of $\alpha$ that $(P;P)\cdot P=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define monochromatic; $P$ is monochromatic so $(P;P)\cdot P=0$.

nodes.name: Part (1): non-representability
nodes.statement: Non representabiliy uses the first partition of $H$. Note that $;$ is defined on ${\mathfrak{Cm}}({\cal F})$ so that $$H^P; H^Q=\bigcup \{H^Z: Z\leq P; Q\in {\bold M}\}.$$ So $\bold M$ is isomorphic to a subalgebra of ${\mathfrak{Cm}} F$. But ${\mathfrak{Cm}} F$ can only be represented on infinite sets, while ${\mathfrak{M}}$ only on finite ones, hence we are done.
nodes.statement_short: $\bold M$ embeds in ${\mathfrak{Cm}}\cal F$; finite vs infinite base contradiction.

nodes.name: Part (2): representability of the term algebra
nodes.statement: The representability of the term algebra uses the second partition. The blow up and blur algebra is ${\cal R}=\{X\subseteq F: X\cap E^W\in Cof(E^W), \forall W\in J\}$. For any $a\in F$ and $W\in J$, let $$U^a=\{X\in R: a\in X\}$$ and $$U^W=\{X\in R: |Z\cap E^W|\geq \omega\}$$ Let $${\sf Uf}=\{U^a: a\in F\}\cup \{U^W: W\in J: |E^W|\geq \omega \}.$$ ${\sf Uf}$ denotes the set of ultrafilters of $\cal R$, that include at least one non-principal ultrafilter, that is an element of the form $U^W$. Let $F,G,K$ be boolean ultrafilters in a relation algebra and let $;$ denote composition. Then $$F;G=\{X;Y: X\in F, Y\in G\}.$$ The triple $(F,G,K)$ is {\it consistent} if the following holds: $$F;G\subseteq K, F;K\subseteq G\text{ and }G;K\subseteq F.$$ So to represent $\cal R$ using $Uf$ as colours, we want to achieve (i) -(iii) below: \begin{enumroman} \item $(U^a,U^b,U^W)$ is consistent whenever $a,b\in H$ and $a;b\in U^W.$ \item $(F,G,K)$ is consistent whenever at least two of $F,G,K$ are non-principal and $F,G,K\in Uf-\{U^{Id}\}.$ \item For any $a,b,c,d\in H$, there is $W\in J'$ such that $a;b\cap c;d\in U^W$. \end{enumroman} Let us see how to represent this algebra. We call $(G,l)$ a {\it consistent coloured graph} if $G$ is a set, $l:G\times G\to Uf$ such that for all $x,y,z\in G$, the following hold: \begin{enumroman} \item $l(x,y)=U^{Id}$ iff $x=y,$ \item $l(x,y)=l(y,x)$ \item The triple $(l(x,y),l(x,z),l(y,z))$ is consistent. \end{enumroman} We say that a consistent coloured graph $(G,l)$ is complete if for all $x,y\in G$, and $F,K\in Uf$, whenever $(l(x,y),F,K)$ is consistent, then there is a node $z$ such that $l(z,x)=F$ and $l(z,y)=K$. We will build a complete consistent graph step-by-step. So assume (inductively) that$(G,l)$ is a consistent coloured graph and $(l(x,y), F, K)$ is a consistent triple. We shall extend $(G,l)$ with a new point $z$ such that $(l(x,y), l(z,x), l(z,y)) =(l(x,y),G,K).$ Let $z\notin G.$ We define $l(z,p)$ for $p\in G$ as follows: $$l(z,x)=F$$ $$l(z,y)=K, \text { and if } p\in G\smallsetminus \{x,y\}, \text { then }$$ $$l(z,p)=U^W\text { for some }W\in J' \text { such that both }$$ $$(U^W, F, l(x,p))\text { and } (U^W, K, l(y,p))\text { are consistent }.$$ Such a $W$ exists by our assumptions (i)-(iii). Conditions (i)-(ii) guarantee that this extension is again a consistent coloured graph. We now show that any non-empty complete coloured graph $(G,l)$ gives a representation for $\cal R.$ For any $X\in R$ define $$rep(X)=\{(u,v)\in G\times G: X\in l(u,v)\}$$ We show that $$rep:{\cal R}\to R(G)$$ is an embedding. $rep$ is a boolean homomorphism because all the labels are ultrafilters. $$rep(Id)=\{(u,u): u\in G\},$$ and for all $X\in R$, $$rep(X)^{-1}=rep(X).$$ The latter follows from the first condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph. From the second condition in the definition of a consistent coloured graph, we have: $$rep(X);rep(Y)\subseteq rep(X;Y).$$ Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X), (v,w)\in rep(Y)$ I.e. $X\in l(u,v), Y\in l(v,w).$ Since $(l(u,v), l(v,w), l(u,w))$ is consistent, then $X;Y\in l(u,w)$, i.e. $(u,w)\in rep(X;Y).$ On the other hand, since $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i)-(ii) hold, we have: $$rep(X;Y)\subseteq rep(X);rep(Y),$$ because $(G,l)$ is complete and because (i) and (ii) hold. Indeed, let $(u,v)\in rep(X;Y)$. Then $X;Y\in l(u,v)$. We show that there are $F,K\in {\sf Uf}$ such that $$X\in F, Y\in K \text { and } (l(u,v), F,K)\text { is consistent }.$$ We distinguish between two cases: {\bf Case 1}. $l(u,v)=U^a$ for some $a\in F$. By $X;Y\in U^a$ we have $a\in X;Y.$ Then there are $b\in X$, $c\in Y$ with $a\leq b;c.$ Then $(U^a, U^b, U^c)$ is consistent. {\bf Case 2.} $l(u,v)=U^W$ for some $W\in J'$. Then $|X;Y\cap E^W|\geq \omega$ by $X;Y\in U^W$. Now if both $X$ and $Y$ are finite, then there are $a\in X$, $b\in Y$ with $|a;b\cap E^W|\geq \omega$. Then $(U^W, U^a, U^b)$ is consistent by (i). Assume that one of $X,Y$, say $X$ is infinite. Let $S\in J'$ such that $|X\cap E^S|\geq \omega$ and let $a\in Y$ be arbitrary. Then $(U^W, U^S, U^a)$ is consistent by (ii) and $X\in U^S, Y\in U^a.$ Finally, $rep$ is one to one because $rep(a)\neq \emptyset$ for all $a\in A$. Indeed $(u,v)\in rep(Id)$ for any $u\in G$. Let $a\in H$. Then $(U^{Id}, U^a, U^a)$ is consistent, so there is a $v\in G$ with $l(u,v)=U^a$. Then $(u,v)\in rep(a).$
nodes.statement_short: Represent $\cal R$ via a complete consistent coloured graph.

nodes.name: Relation algebra case via F(i,1)
nodes.statement: {Proof} For the second we use the second construction. Let ${\cal D}$ be a non- trivial ultraproduct of the atom structures ${\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$. Then ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal D}$ is completely representable. Thus ${\mathfrak{Tm}}{\cal F}(i,1)$ are ${\sf RRA}$'s without a complete representation while their ultraproduct has a complete representation. Also ${\mathfrak{Cm}}{\cal F}(i,1)$, $i\in \omega$ are non representable with a completely representable ultraproduct. This yields the desired result.
nodes.section: The analogy, first informaly, then formally in a map
nodes.statement_short: Ultraproduct of ${\cal F}(i,1)$ is completely representable.

nodes.name: Cylindric case via cliques
nodes.statement: We prove the cylindric case. Take ${\bf G}_i$ to be the disjoint union of cliques of size $n(n-1)/2+i$. Let $\alpha_i$ be the corresponding atom astructure of ${\mathfrak{A}}_i$, as constructed above. Then ${\mathfrak{Cm}} {\mathfrak{A}}_i$ is not representable, but $\prod_{i\in \omega}{\mathfrak{Cm}}{\mathfrak{A}}_i={\mathfrak{Cm}}(\prod_{i\in \omega}{\mathfrak{A}}_i)$. Then the latter is based on the disjoint union of the cliques which is arbitrarily large, hence is representable.

nodes.statement_short: Use cliques of size $n(n-1)/2+i$; the ultraproduct is representable.
